preview: Naman Gosain shares his interview experience for the Intern Analyst role at Wells Fargo, detailing the online assessment, two technical rounds, and the HR interview.
content: Wells Fargo Intern Analyst Interview experience Duration - 8 weeks (2 months) Stipend - 90,000/- per month Location - Bangalore/Hyderabad Naman Gosain Computer Engineering Batch - 2026 Introduction Hey everyone! I’m super excited to share my interview experience with Wells Fargo, and I hope it helps you in your placement journey too. So, a little about the company first — Wells Fargo is one of the top 4 banks in the United States, and trust me, it’s a big name in the finance and tech world. When we heard that Wells Fargo was finally coming for intern analyst roles, there was a wave of excitement across campus. It came a bit late in the placement season, and we were honestly starting to get worried that it might not show up at all. But once the registration link dropped, there was this collective “Finally!” feeling among all of us. The registration process was simple, and the selection process had a clear structure: one Online Assessment (OA) round followed by three interviews – two technical and one HR. It felt a bit intense seeing three rounds lined up, but since it was Wells Fargo, we were all geared up. This interview experience turned out to be a mix of challenges, surprises, and some really cool learning moments. So, if you're someone looking to land an internship at a major firm, I hope my story gives you some insights (and maybe a little confidence boost too!). Online Assessment (OA) Now let’s talk about the Online Assessment — honestly, it was quite a mix of everything! Wells Fargo didn’t want to leave any area untouched. This OA was conducted offline on 22nd April 2025, which honestly added its own kind of pressure. You know that feeling when you're not just competing with logic but also with the silence in the room? Yep, that one. The assessment had English comprehension, aptitude, a graph-based stock analysis section, a few basic Gen AI questions (which I really didn’t expect!), and three coding questions. Quite the combo platter, right? The English section was mostly standard stuff — comprehension, synonyms, arranging the sentences in correct order, sentence correction, paragraph related questions — you know, the usual suspects. But at one point, the options were so close that I started second-guessing my entire understanding of grammar. I'm pretty sure I stared at one sentence for a solid minute trying to decide if it sounded right or was actually right. Then came the stock-based graph analysis section, and boy, that felt like I was suddenly working at Bloomberg. They gave a stock price chart and threw questions like, “When was the price highest?”, “Which day had the steepest drop?”, and I was like — Wait, am I giving an OA or preparing to become a stock trader?? It was interesting, though, and definitely different from the usual aptitude rounds. Oh, and just when I thought I had seen it all — a few simple Gen AI questions popped up! Things like identifying AI applications, understanding basic AI logic, and I was like “Umm... okay, didn’t study for this but let’s go!” And then... the coding part arrived — with its own twist. Three coding questions, but one of them was sitting mysteriously under a different heading: “FTE Wellness.” Still not sure what was "well" about it, but okay Wells Fargo, we trust your vibes. Coding Questions – The Real Deal Okay, now let’s dive into the coding section — probably the part everyone’s most curious about! Like I mentioned earlier, there were three coding questions, and for some reason, one of them was tucked away in a completely different section called “FTE Wellness”. Still no idea why they put it there — maybe solving it was supposed to make us feel “well”? Anyway, here’s how it went down: ● Question 1 – The Warmup The first question was honestly a breeze. I can’t recall the exact problem (classic moment, right?), but I do remember solving it within 5–7 minutes. It was very easy, probably something basic with arrays or strings. Definitely a good confidence booster to start off with. ● Question 2 – Frequency Sort This one was more interesting. We were given a list of numbers with multiple occurrences, and the task was to arrange them in decreasing order of their frequency. If two numbers had the same frequency, we had to maintain their original order of appearance in the list. The moment I read the problem, I was like "Ohhh okay, this looks fancy but not too bad." I quickly thought of using a hashmap to store frequencies and then sorting based on that, with a touch of stable sorting to maintain order. Solved it without much trouble and was feeling pretty good about it. ● Question 3 – Cryptarithmetic Chaos Ah yes, the final boss of the OA – a cryptarithmetic puzzle. And not the cute ones with SEND + MORE = MONEY. This one meant business. The logic was okay to grasp, but it involved a lot of permutations and backtracking. I tried optimizing as much as I could, but sadly, the last two test cases kept failing due to time limits. Not gonna lie, it was a little frustrating because I knew the logic was right — it was just the execution speed that wasn’t keeping up. Still, I was proud I gave it a solid shot. And considering the rest of the OA had gone well, I was hopeful. Technical Interview 1 This round happened on 29th April 2025, in online mode, and went on for about 30–35 minutes. It was one of those interviews that started off like a regular technical round but slowly turned into a fun blend of technical + HR — like the interviewer was trying to see how I think and who I am as a person. As expected, we began with the classic: “Tell me about yourself as I go through your resume.” I had practiced this part, so I was comfortable. But what really made me smile was what came next. He looked at my project and said: “This TradeSphere looks catchy. What is it?” And that was my moment! I explained what the project was, why I built it, and why such an application is actually needed. He seemed genuinely interested and started giving me scenario-based questions like: ● “Suppose your scraper fails because the website now asks for a captcha. What would you do?” ● “If your data source crashes unexpectedly, how would you handle it?” To be honest, I was able to answer all the scenarios confidently, because yep — I actually built the project myself and didn’t just copy it off GitHub or some random blog (That’s why you should always know what’s on your resume!) Then came the surprise twist. He suddenly said: “Since you’ve worked with MongoDB, let me give you a Mongo query.” I was like — "Wait what? MongoDB query in an interview?" People usually ask SQL, right? (BTW, till now, all my Mongo queries were mostly written by ChatGPT) But I gave it a shot, wrote something that made sense logically. Just to go the extra mile, I even wrote the SQL version of the same query right after — wanted to show that I understood both. He then moved to some OOPs basics — asked me to explain: ● The 4 pillars of OOP ● What’s an abstract class ● What’s an interface That part was pretty chill, and I handled it well. But the real highlight was toward the end. He suddenly said: “What is Naman?” And I, totally confused, replied: “Naman means Namaskaar...” He burst out laughing and said: “No no, I meant — who is Naman? What kind of person are you?” I laughed along thinking what have I even done, but I gathered myself and answered genuinely. He wrapped it up by asking: “What’s your motivation behind what you do?” Overall, it felt like more than just a tech grilling — it was a conversation where he tried to understand me technically and personally. A really refreshing experience, to be honest. Out of 25 people I got selected for the next round. Technical Interview 2 This interview took place on 10th May 2025, again in online mode, and lasted for about 30 minutes. But this one started off with a surprise. Some person joined the call and casually said: “Naman, please wait for 5 minutes, the Executive Director will be joining soon.” And I was like — "Whaaaaat? Executive Director??" Cue mini heart attack. I mean, it’s not every day you casually chat with someone that high up, so yes, I was a little nervous... but I quickly told myself: “You’ve got this.” He joined and started just like the previous round — “Tell me about yourself.” After that, he asked me basic questions like: “What is Operating System?”, “What is Computer Networks?” All good till here. But then he goes: “Let’s make things a little more interesting…” That line is never not scary in an interview. He said, “If you had a superpower, and you could keep only one subject — OS or CN — which one would you keep?” I took a second to think and replied OS. I explained that the OS acts like the heart of the system, managing processes, memory, threads, and acting as the foundation layer between hardware and software. Without an OS, nothing really "runs" — it's the base that keeps everything ticking. He smiled and jumped in: “But CN has enabled global communication, the internet, cloud... don’t you think CN has revolutionized everything?” And I totally agreed with him — CN has taken us from isolated machines to a connected world. But I stood my ground and said: “Even with all the advancements in CN, without a stable OS underneath, those systems wouldn't even function. OS is what lets CN happen in the first place.” That seemed to satisfy him, and the nervousness started fading away. Then he asked about the projects I had worked on. I walked him through all three on my resume. And no surprise — his attention locked onto TradeSphere again (of course, it's a bank — so anything with stocks is like magnet). He asked: “There are so many existing applications for stock analysis. Why did you make another one?” I said, “Because unless we build something ourselves, we never truly understand how it works underneath. I wanted to learn by doing — not just by reading or using apps built by others.” That hit the mark. Then came the wildest question of all: “If you were to make a Naman Indicator, how would you design it?” I blinked. Literally sat there like for a second. But then the creativity kicked in. I said something like: “First, I’d identify what kind of investor Naman is — short-term, long-term, or intraday. Based on that, I’d adjust the weights on technical indicators like the 50-day and 200-day EMAs, maybe even add RSI or MACD. For example, if he’s a long-term investor, I’d put more weight on the 200-day EMA and trends over months. If he’s into short-term trading, I’d factor in volatility-based indicators. So basically, I’d design a custom weighted moving average system that adapts to the person’s behavior.” He nodded with a satisfied smile, and I was really happy with that answer. I could tell it made a solid impression. Finally, he asked some behavioral questions: “Can you work in a team?” “What if you have to work alone?” I answered both honestly, giving examples of both scenarios. And with that, we wrapped up. To be honest — this round was unexpected, slightly intimidating, but also really enjoyable. I walked away feeling happy and confident with how it went. Out of 12 people I was lucky to be selected for the next round. HR Interview The final round — the HR interview — came with a mini jump scare of its own. It was 12th May 2025, around 3:30 PM, when I received a call from someone from the HR Talent Acquisition team. They said: “Hi Naman, can we schedule your HR interview today at 6 PM?” And I was like — “Of course, yes!” (I mean, come on, who says no to HR?) The interview happened online and lasted about 20 minutes, but it was a nice, chill conversation — more about getting to know me than grilling me. He started with a casual tone: “How are you? And tell me honestly — were you free or just said yes out of fear?” I laughed and said I was actually free — no fake bravado needed! Then he asked for my CGPA, about my 12th and 10th marks, and I could hear the keyboard sounds in the background — so pretty sure he was noting things down. The next few questions were classic HR stuff: ● “Why do you want to join Wells Fargo?” ● “What are your weaknesses?” ● “How can you contribute to Wells Fargo?” I answered them honestly, connecting my skills, interest in finance-tech, and what I hoped to learn from such a big company. Then he suddenly asked: “Have you ever lived outside Maharashtra?” I said I hadn’t, just traveled outside a few times. So he told me, “Since our offices are in Bangalore and Hyderabad, you’d have to move — would you be okay with that?” I confidently said yes, and told him I was open to exploring new places and was confident in my ability to adapt to different environments. Toward the end, he said something that lit up my day: “We’re planning to start the internship from 9th June. Would you be okay with that?” That’s when I felt like — this might actually be happening. I had a huge smile and said yes without hesitation. But then came the waiting game. The results didn’t come for days, and honestly, everyone was super tensed. We kept checking, hoping, overthinking… Finally, on 19th May, the results were out — and guess what? I was one of the 5 people selected for the internship! Felt like all the effort, prep, and genuine answers had finally paid off. Tips (That Aren’t Really “Tips”) To be honest, tips are just things people say based on their experiences — but I genuinely believe everyone should develop their own will and way of doing things. What works for me might not work for you, and that’s completely okay! So nope, I’m not gonna throw a list of “Top 10 ways to crack an interview” at you. I believe in keeping things simple — that’s exactly how I approached all my interviews, and trust me, it helped. The moment you start overcomplicating things, you’ll confuse yourself more than the interviewer ever could. Here are just a few thoughts from someone who’s been through it: ● Know your resume — like really, really know it. Please don’t put things just to make it look good. That random “blockchain certification” from 2022? If you don’t remember what it even means now, maybe leave it off. Put stuff you can speak about confidently. Trust me, it matters. ● Know your projects in and out. As you saw in my case, both technical interviews circled back to my project, and since I actually built it myself, I could answer everything easily. So, whatever you’ve built — own it. Debug it. Break it. Fix it. Repeat. ● Be confident and don’t be scared. It’s not just what you say — it’s how you say it. Speak clearly, be honest, and don’t get thrown off if the interviewer laughs or goes off-script. (Looking at you, "What is Naman?" guy) ● Keep learning and keep improving. If you get rejected, don’t get sad. Okay fine, get sad for 15 minutes, eat some chocolate, and then get up and figure out what went wrong. Every interview is a step closer to the one that’s meant for you. Just don’t stop. In the end, all I want to say is — All the best !! Keep working hard, keep it real, and success will follow.
